description: We are building the Lunar Landing Site Navigator to identify safe, high-value landing zones on the Moon using lunar topography, slope, illumination, and hazard data. Looking for motivated teammates with skills in Python, geospatial/GIS analysis, machine learning, data visualization, or UI/UX design. Whether you specialize in space data processing, backend development, or storytelling, join us to build an intuitive navigation and site-selection tool!
summary:
The lunar South Pole is the next frontier of exploration, yet landing there is unusually hard: sunlight is scarce, and the Earth can sit low in the sky or vanish behind terrain, so a poor choice of site or date could leave a lander without power or contact. To help planners decide with confidence, we developed LUNARIS, a working FlutterFlow mobile app that answers two questions together: where should a spacecraft land, and when? For each lunar landing site, it shows sunlight, direct Earth visibility and terrain slope, and combines them into a transparent suitability score weighted 40, 30 and 30, with the full breakdown visible. Site C1 (89.78° S, 128.50° E), for example, shows 86.4% sunlight, 78.2% Earth visibility, a 7.2% slope and a score of 74/100.

NASA data is the core of the timing analysis. The app fetches live information from NASA's JPL Horizons API and CelesTrak and counts when the Sun and Earth stay above the horizon; across 29 six-hour samples from 1 to 8 January 2026, it counted 174.0 hours of Sun and 150.0 hours of geometric Earth visibility. These results are a preliminary screening, not a certified safety assessment. We hope LUNARIS gives students, educators and early planners a clear first look at where and when a lunar landing works best.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

When we read about landing near the lunar South Pole, one challenge stood out to us: sunlight is scarce there, and the Earth can sit low in the sky or hide behind terrain. So we built LUNARIS, a mobile app that helps planners answer two questions together: where should a spacecraft land, and when?

For each lunar landing site, the app shows how much sunlight it receives, how well it can see the Earth directly, and how steep the terrain is. It combines these three measures into one suitability score out of 100, weighted 40% for sunlight, 30% for Earth visibility and 30% for slope, and it keeps the full breakdown on screen so users can see how each score was reached. Site C1 (89.78° S, 128.50° E), for example, shows 86.4% sunlight, 78.2% Earth visibility, a 7.2% slope and a score of 74/100, made up of 34.6, 23.5 and 15.6 points.

For timing, the app connects to NASA's JPL Horizons API (DE441 ephemeris) and CelesTrak and fetches live data. It then counts the hours in which the Sun and the Earth are above the horizon. In our live run for 1 to 8 January 2026, it used 29 six-hour samples and counted 174.0 hours of Sun and 150.0 hours of geometric Earth visibility.

What benefits does it have?

LUNARIS turns complex orbital data into one clear, explainable view. Students, educators and early-stage mission planners can screen landing sites and dates without specialist software, and they can see exactly why a site scores well or poorly. The app also keeps site quality and timing together, which saves users from comparing them separately.

What is the intended impact of the project?

We hope LUNARIS makes lunar landing planning easier to understand and more open to people who are just starting to explore it. By helping planners narrow their options before any deeper analysis begins, it supports clearer and better-informed early decisions for future missions to the lunar South Pole.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

We built the app in FlutterFlow, which produces Flutter code in the Dart language. The app fetches live data through REST API calls to NASA's JPL Horizons system, ISRO data and CelesTrak. We ran, tested and screen-recorded the app on smartphones, and we produced the demo video with Python (Pillow, NumPy and OpenCV) and ffmpeg.

How is your project creative?

Most approaches treat the landing site and the landing date as two separate questions. We wanted to bring them together in one app, so LUNARIS shows its scoring openly instead of hiding it behind a single number, and it relies on live NASA data rather than fixed tables.

What factors did your team consider?

We gave sunlight the largest weight because a lander depends on it for power, while Earth visibility and slope each carry 30% because they affect communication and landing safety. We also decided to label our results honestly: Earth visibility is geometric, not a verified radio link, and the score is a preliminary screening, not a certified safety assessment.
